name: Homemade Extruded Pasta with Sunday Gravy

elevations.instruction: Build the gravy in three waves, not one pot-dump. First, brown the pork neck bones or country ribs hard in a dry Dutch oven until mahogany, then remove. Sear the meatballs in the rendered fat until a crust forms, remove. Only then do you soften onions and garlic, toast a heaping tablespoon of tomato paste in the fat until it smells like pizza and turns brick-red (2-3 minutes), deglaze with a splash of dry red wine, and add two 28-oz cans of San Marzanos crushed by hand. Return all the meat, partial lid, and simmer on the lowest possible flame for 3-4 hours. Skim the fat that pools on top twice during cooking.
elevations.rationale: Sunday gravy is a fond-building exercise disguised as a tomato sauce. Every stage contributes a different browned note: the pork bones give you collagen and a porky backbone, the meatball sear gives you caramelized beef, and the toasted tomato paste contributes that deep, sweet, almost-burnt sugar quality that separates restaurant red sauce from weeknight marinara. Skimming the fat is what keeps it from tasting greasy after four hours.

elevations.instruction: Finish the extruded spinach pasta IN the gravy, not under it. Cook the pasta 60 seconds shy of al dente, reserve a full cup of the starchy cooking water, then transfer the pasta directly into a wide sauté pan with two ladles of gravy (not the meat) and a splash of pasta water. Toss vigorously over medium heat for 90 seconds until the sauce goes from watery to glossy and clingy. Plate the pasta first, then crown with the meats and a final spoon of gravy on top.
elevations.rationale: Fresh extruded spinach pasta has a porous, slightly rough surface that was engineered to grab sauce. Finishing it in the pan lets the pasta absorb the tomato flavor from the inside while the starch emulsifies the oil and tomato into a single glossy coating. Keeping the meats for the top preserves the image of Sunday dinner and keeps the meatballs from falling apart in the toss.

elevations.instruction: Serve with a bowl of garlicky toasted breadcrumbs (pangrattato) on the table. Tear a few slices of day-old country bread into coarse crumbs, toast in a skillet with 3 tablespoons olive oil, 2 smashed garlic cloves, and a pinch of red pepper flake until deep golden and fragrant, then toss with lemon zest and torn parsley. Pass at the table for everyone to shower on top.
elevations.rationale: Long-simmered sauce and soft fresh pasta both live on the tender-and-saucy end of the spectrum. A crunchy, savory, lemony breadcrumb is the classic southern Italian answer to Parmigiano for sauces like this. It adds crunch, a second hit of garlic, and a citrus lift that makes the third forkful taste as exciting as the first.

name: Steak & Romaine Salad with Cucumbers, Red Onions, and Avocados

elevations.instruction: Dry-brine the steak the moment you take it out of the package that morning: pat it dry, season aggressively with kosher salt and cracked black pepper on every surface, and set it uncovered on a rack in the fridge all day. When you are ready to cook, pull it out, let it rest on the counter while a cast-iron screams over high heat, then sear 2-3 minutes per side for medium-rare, rest 8 minutes, slice against the grain.
elevations.rationale: A day-long dry brine does three things while you're at busy workday: salt penetrates and seasons the meat throughout, surface moisture evaporates so the steak sears instantly instead of steaming, and enzymes gently tenderize the fibers. You walk in at dinner time, and dinner is 15 minutes away with zero active prep.

elevations.instruction: Quick-pickle the red onions while the pan heats up. Thinly slice half a red onion, toss with 3 tablespoons red wine vinegar, a teaspoon of sugar, a pinch of salt, and let them sit for 10 minutes. The onions turn hot pink, lose their harshness, and the leftover brine becomes half of your salad dressing. Whisk that vinegar brine with 5 tablespoons olive oil, a teaspoon of Dijon, and cracked pepper.
elevations.rationale: Raw red onion is too aggressive this late at night, and acid is exactly what a rich, salty seared steak begs for. Pickled onions solve both problems at once and make the bowl look like it came off a restaurant pass. Using the brine as dressing means zero waste and one fewer step.

elevations.instruction: Keep the romaine ice-cold and the steak hot when they meet. Tear (do not chop) the romaine into big rustic pieces, hold in a bowl over ice or in the fridge until the last second. Slice the steak while still hot and fan it directly over the cold greens, cucumbers, and avocado so the warm juices and beef fat start to wilt and dress the bottom layer of lettuce.
elevations.rationale: The textbook steakhouse wedge plays on this exact contrast. Cold crunchy romaine against hot, juicy steak is what makes every bite feel dynamic instead of just salad-with-meat. The warm beef juices become a second dressing that carries the pickled-onion vinaigrette into every leaf.

elevations.instruction: Finish the pasta in the sauce. Pull the babo from the boiling water 60 seconds early, while the center is still ever-so-slightly chalky, and transfer it directly into the sauté pan with the brown butter and ½ cup of the starchy cooking water. Toss vigorously over medium heat for 60-90 seconds until the sauce turns from broken and greasy-looking to glossy and cream-like as it clings to every strand.
elevations.rationale: This is the single most important technique in Italian pasta cooking, and it was designed for delicate fresh pasta like babo. The starch in the cooking water acts as a natural emulsifier, binding butter and water into a sauce that coats instead of slides. You will never have a puddle of melted butter at the bottom of the bowl again.

elevations.instruction: Brown 5 tablespoons of unsalted butter in a light-colored pan over medium heat until the milk solids turn deep amber and the butter smells like toasted hazelnuts, about 4 minutes. The instant it's done, toss in 12-15 fresh sage leaves. They will crackle and crisp in 10 seconds. Pour the whole thing over the finished pasta with a small squeeze of lemon and a heavy shower of Parmigiano-Reggiano grated on a Microplane.
elevations.rationale: The egg-yolk-only dough is rich, custardy, and almost pastry-like. Brown butter amplifies that richness with a nutty, toasty depth, while the sage contributes an earthy savory-sweet note that plays off the spinach. The squeeze of lemon at the end is the secret — a tiny hit of acid keeps the whole bowl from feeling heavy and makes every bite taste bright.

elevations.instruction: Finish with a tablespoon of toasted pine nuts or coarsely chopped walnuts, dry-toasted in a small pan until fragrant, then tossed with flaky salt. Scatter over the plated pasta along with a few crispy sage leaves you set aside from the brown butter.
elevations.rationale: Fresh egg-yolk pasta is as tender as pudding, and brown butter coats everything in softness. A scatter of toasted nuts and shattered sage leaves provides the textural counterpunch that transforms each bite from a single note into a chord.

name: Pan-Fried Pork Dumplings + Garlic Sesame Noodles with Bok Choy

elevations.instruction: Use the proper pan-fry-steam-fry technique for the dumplings: heat 2 tablespoons neutral oil in a nonstick skillet over medium-high, arrange the frozen dumplings flat-side down in a tight circle, and let them sear undisturbed for 2 minutes until the bottoms are deep golden. Pour in ⅓ cup water plus a teaspoon of cornstarch slurry, immediately cover with a tight lid, and steam for 6-7 minutes. Uncover, let the remaining water evaporate, and listen for the sizzle to go silent before flipping out onto a plate, crust-side up.
elevations.rationale: Frozen dumplings fail because home cooks either steam them soggy or fry them raw inside. This three-phase method is the same one used in Beijing jiaozi shops: the sear builds a crust, the covered steam cooks the filling through, and the final dry-fry with the cornstarch slurry creates a lacy, crackling 'snowflake' crust that's the signature of a proper guotie. It takes 10 minutes and the result looks like a restaurant plate.

elevations.instruction: Upgrade the garlic sesame noodle sauce by toasting aromatics in the oil first. In a small pot, heat ⅓ cup neutral oil with 3 thinly sliced garlic cloves and 1 tablespoon of grated fresh ginger over medium-low until the garlic is just pale gold. Pour the hot oil over 3 tablespoons toasted sesame paste (or tahini) whisked with 3 tablespoons soy sauce, 2 tablespoons Chinkiang black vinegar, 1 tablespoon sugar, and 1 teaspoon toasted sesame oil. The sizzle blooms the aromatics into the sauce.
elevations.rationale: Pouring hot aromatic oil over sesame paste is the classic Sichuan move for dan dan and liangmian. It does two things at once: it cooks the raw garlic and ginger just enough to tame the harsh bite, and it emulsifies the thick sesame paste into a silky, pourable sauce. Chinkiang vinegar is the non-negotiable ingredient — it adds a smoky, malty depth that rice vinegar can't match.

elevations.instruction: Keep the bok choy crunchy and separate the stems from the leaves. Halve baby bok choy lengthwise, blanch stems-down in salted boiling water for 60 seconds, then flip and submerge the leaves for 20 seconds more. Shock in ice water, pat bone dry. Toss into the warm noodles at the very end with a shower of sliced scallions, toasted sesame seeds, and torn cilantro.
elevations.rationale: Stir-fried bok choy in sesame noodles always ends up limp and watery because the leaves and stems cook at wildly different rates. Blanching and shocking preserves the snap of the stems, the bright green of the leaves, and keeps water out of the sauce. The raw scallions and cilantro at the end add a sharp, fresh lift that cuts through the rich sesame.

elevations.instruction: Preheat a baking steel or inverted heavy sheet pan on the lowest rack at 550°F (or your oven's max) for a full 45 minutes before the first pizza goes in. Cold-ferment the dough for 24-72 hours in the fridge after its initial rise — pull each dough ball out 90 minutes before stretching. Stretch by hand on a semolina-dusted peel, dress fast, and launch immediately. Each pie should bake in 5-7 minutes with leopard spots on the underside.
elevations.rationale: Home pizza fails because the oven isn't hot enough and the dough hasn't developed flavor. A preheated steel conducts heat six times better than a cold sheet pan, which is what gives you a blistered, crackling bottom and a puffy cornicione. Long cold fermentation lets the gluten relax and the yeast produce complex, slightly sour, almost-beery flavor notes that no same-day dough can match.

elevations.instruction: Make an uncooked pizza sauce: blitz one 28-oz can of whole San Marzanos with 2 tablespoons olive oil, 1 teaspoon kosher salt, a pinch of sugar, 1 grated garlic clove, and a torn basil stem in a food processor for 5 seconds — you want it chunky, not smooth. Do NOT cook it before topping the pizza. Keep mozzarella fresh, torn into chunks (not shredded bagged), patted bone dry on paper towels for 15 minutes before topping.
elevations.rationale: Cooked pizza sauce turns muddy and sweet in the short oven time. An uncooked sauce delivers the bright, almost raw-tomato tang you taste at a great Neapolitan pizzeria. Wet pre-shredded mozzarella is pizza's worst enemy — the moisture boils off and leaves you with soupy toppings. Hand-torn fresh mozz that's been dried gives you molten pools instead of a puddle.

elevations.instruction: Finish each pie after it leaves the oven, not before. Pizza Margherita gets a thread of good extra-virgin olive oil and torn fresh basil the moment it lands. A white pizza gets a squeeze of lemon and cracked black pepper. A hot honey pizza gets its honey drizzle at the table, not on the dough. Always serve with a bowl of lemony arugula on the side, dressed with olive oil and shaved Parmigiano.
elevations.rationale: High-heat baking destroys delicate flavors like raw basil, good olive oil, and lemon. Adding them after the bake means they hit the tongue in their intended state, bright and perfumed, rather than cooked to sludge. The arugula salad is the classic Italian foil to rich, cheesy pizza — it resets the palate between slices.

name: Whole Roasted Branzino with Sautéed Kale and Creamy Polenta

elevations.instruction: Score the branzino three times on each side, cutting through the skin and just into the flesh at a 45-degree angle. Stuff the belly cavity with lemon slices, fresh thyme, a crushed garlic clove, and a pinch of fennel seed. Pat the skin completely dry, brush generously with olive oil, and season heavily with kosher salt inside and out. Roast on a preheated sheet pan at 450°F for 18-22 minutes until the skin is blistered and the flesh at the backbone flakes easily with a fork.
elevations.rationale: Scoring the skin does two things: it keeps the fish from curling in the heat and it creates more surface area for the skin to crisp. The stuffed aromatics gently steam the interior from the inside out while the high-heat dry roast delivers papery, shatteringly crisp skin — the whole reason you bother with a whole fish instead of a fillet.

elevations.instruction: Make a 5-minute salsa verde while the fish roasts: finely chop 1 cup packed flat-leaf parsley, 2 tablespoons capers, 2 anchovy fillets, 1 small garlic clove, and the zest of 1 lemon. Stir together with ½ cup good olive oil, the juice of half a lemon, and a pinch of red pepper flake. Spoon generously over the carved fish at the table.
elevations.rationale: Whole roasted fish needs a bright, herbaceous, briny counterpoint — the default for Italian coastal kitchens is salsa verde for exactly this reason. The capers and anchovies deliver salty, savory depth that reinforces the sea flavor of the fish, and the raw garlic and lemon cut through the richness of the crispy skin. It transforms a simple roasted fish into a composed plate.

elevations.instruction: Treat the polenta and the kale as deliberate opposites. Make the polenta extra-creamy: stone-ground cornmeal cooked low and slow in a 5:1 liquid-to-meal ratio (half milk, half water or stock) for 35-40 minutes, finished with 3 tablespoons butter and ½ cup grated Parmigiano off the heat. The kale should be aggressive: hot pan, olive oil, 2 smashed garlic cloves, red pepper flake, and the kale tossed in for 3 minutes so the edges crisp and char while the centers stay toothsome. Squeeze lemon on before plating.
elevations.rationale: A great plate is a texture map. The polenta gives you pillowy creaminess (like a sauce that happens to be a starch), the kale gives you charred, slightly bitter, chewy chew, and the fish gives you flaky tender flesh with a crispy skin. Three distinct textures on one plate is what makes restaurant food feel composed.

elevations.instruction: Toast the tortillas one at a time directly over a gas flame (or in a dry cast-iron skillet over high heat) for 15-20 seconds per side, just until they puff slightly and pick up a few charred spots. Wrap the warm tortillas in a clean kitchen towel inside a tortilla warmer or zip-top bag so they stay pliable and steam gently while you set the rest of the table.
elevations.rationale: Room-temperature tortillas taste like cardboard. A quick char over open flame is the single biggest flavor upgrade you can make for taco night — it wakes up the corn, adds smoky depth, and turns a floppy disc into something that tastes like it came off a Mexico City grill. Elsie will love watching the tortillas puff. It is a thirty-second parenting win.

elevations.instruction: Build a proper taco bar with three finishing sauces, each in its own small bowl: (1) a creamy avocado-cilantro crema (1 avocado, ¼ cup sour cream, handful of cilantro, juice of 1 lime, pinch of salt, blitzed smooth), (2) a quick charred salsa roja (char 4 Roma tomatoes, half an onion, and 2 garlic cloves under the broiler for 8 minutes, blend with a chipotle in adobo and salt), and (3) a 10-minute pickled red onion with lime juice instead of vinegar for a softer acidity Elsie will actually eat.
elevations.rationale: The secret to a great taco is layering three textures of sauce: creamy, tangy-spicy, and acidic-crunchy. Giving an 8-year-old her own little bowls to spoon from turns dinner into a project she's in charge of, and solo dads know that autonomy at the table is the difference between 'I don't like this' and 'look what I made.' Bonus: every one of these sauces keeps for 3 days in the fridge.

elevations.instruction: Set up a crunch bar alongside the proteins: a bowl of quick-pickled onions, a bowl of crumbled queso fresco or cotija, a bowl of shredded romaine or cabbage dressed with lime, a bowl of diced cucumber and radish tossed with salt, a bowl of toasted pepitas or crushed plain tortilla chips for scattering on top, and quartered limes for squeezing. Keep proteins simple — a skillet of seasoned ground beef or turkey and a skillet of crisped seasoned black beans — so the toppings are the star.
elevations.rationale: The joy of build-your-own for a kid is the combinatorial math. Six toppings, two proteins, and three sauces is effectively unlimited tacos for Elsie to design, and every one of them has crunch, creaminess, and acid built in by default. It also means you cook two things, not twelve, and the whole meal feels like a party with a table full of color.
